# **1** Project summary {-#project-summary}

This report presents the outcomes of *Refining Species and Disturbance in EFRI Inventories*, a project funded by the Knowledge Transfer and Tool Development (KTTD) program of the Forestry Futures Trust and led by Université Laval. The project developed and tested an automated workflow that turns wall-to-wall LiDAR data into forest stand polygons ready for inventory and planning. The workflow:

1. delineates stands automatically from single-photon LiDAR (SPL) metrics;
2. attributes each stand with LiDAR-derived forest attributes, recent disturbances, stand age and land cover;
3. accepts species composition from any compatible map product.

The workflow was applied to two contrasting forest management units (FMUs): the boreal Romeo Malette Forest (RMF) and the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Ottawa Valley Forest (OVF). The automated stands were compared with the photo-interpreted Forest Resources Inventory (FRI) polygons, using independent high-resolution reference data collected with drone LiDAR and field plots.

The project delivers attributed polygon layers covering both FMUs, the open-source R package [eFRItools](https://github.com/metafor-ulaval/eFRItools), an interactive viewer, and this report (see [Deliverables and tools](deliverables.qmd)).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Key findings

- **Automated stands are at least as good as photo-interpreted stands.** Delineations built from SPL metrics produced stands that were more internally uniform than FRI polygons (within-stand variability reduced by up to 8.6%) and that captured more of the structural variation of the landscape (up to +9.2 percentage points of variance explained).
- **Their boundaries follow real changes in forest structure, especially in mixed forests.** In OVF, boundaries of SPL-based delineations matched LiDAR-detected structural transitions markedly better than FRI boundaries (F1-score 8.5% to 35.9% higher). In RMF, where stand edges are sharper and easier to photo-interpret, the "SPL only" delineation performed as well as or better than the FRI.
- **LiDAR structure is the key input.** Delineations based on Sentinel-2 imagery alone performed worse than the FRI on every criterion. Adding a Sentinel-2 red-edge band to SPL metrics helped in the mixed forest of OVF, but not in the boreal RMF.
- **One configuration works in both units.** The "SPL only" delineation, which needs only the provincial SPL data, was the most consistent across units and was used to produce the final polygon layers.
- **The automated layers are operationally plausible.** Segmentation parameters were calibrated so that polygon size and shape resemble FRI polygons. The final layers contain 73,670 polygons in RMF (FRI: 79,094) and 55,291 in OVF (FRI: 68,169).
:::

# **2** Project context {-#project-context}

Forest management planning in Ontario relies on stand polygons. The FRI describes the composition, age, height and stocking of each stand, and planners use these polygons for reporting, growth and yield projections, and operational decisions. FRI polygons are delineated by aerial photo-interpretation, which is time-consuming, partly subjective, and difficult to repeat often over large FMUs. Between updates, harvesting, natural disturbances and stand development make parts of the inventory outdated.

Ontario's leaf-on SPL program now provides wall-to-wall LiDAR coverage and derived enhanced forest inventory (EFI) products, such as canopy height, merchantable volume, basal area and stem density, mapped on a 20 m grid. These rasters describe forest structure in much more detail than polygons, but planners still need polygons. The challenge is to turn raster products into stands that are internally uniform, distinct from their neighbours, and bounded where forest structure actually changes.

# **3** Previous work {-#previous-work}

This project builds on an earlier Forestry Futures Trust project led by the University of British Columbia with GreenFirst Forest Products, the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Université Laval ([Berman et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1080/07038992.2024.2391319)). That project showed that Generic Region Merging (GRM) segmentation of LiDAR metrics can produce stand-like polygons that reflect current forest structure better than older FRI polygons in some areas. It also showed that interpreted attributes such as species composition and age can be transferred from FRI polygons to the new polygons by imputation.

Four issues remained before the approach could be used operationally:

- polygons needed sizes and shapes closer to those expected in operational inventories;
- the approach had been developed mainly in boreal conditions and needed testing in other forest types;
- disturbance history, stand age and species composition needed updating where the FRI no longer reflected current conditions;
- polygon quality needed to be assessed with objective criteria rather than by visual comparison with FRI maps.

On the last point, a useful stand map must do more than produce uniform polygons. It must also separate structurally different areas and place boundaries where forest structure changes. These three criteria guided the evaluation carried out in this project.

# **4** Project objectives {-#project-objectives}

The overall objective was to refine the automated delineation and attribution workflow so that it can support the modernization of Ontario's forest inventory. The specific objectives were to:

1. **Refine the automated segmentation.** Adjust the segmentation so that it transfers across forest types and produces polygons whose size, shape and structural content are compatible with FRI products.

2. **Integrate LiDAR-derived EFI attributes.** Summarize wall-to-wall EFI rasters (height, volume, basal area, density and canopy cover) within the new polygons.

3. **Incorporate disturbance and age information.** Use provincial and national disturbance and age products to update polygons where recent harvests or fires are missing from the FRI.

4. **Keep species composition flexible.** The original proposal planned to improve the imputation of species composition. Gains from imputation proved limited, while a parallel project using deep learning showed stronger potential for mapping species. The workflow was therefore designed to take species composition from any compatible raster product, including future deep learning outputs, rather than from a single imputation method.

5. **Evaluate the quality of automated stands** with three complementary criteria: internal homogeneity of stands, partitioning of structural variability among stands, and correspondence of stand boundaries with independently detected structural transitions.

# **5** Study area {-#introduction-study-area}

The workflow was tested in two FMUs chosen for their contrasting forest conditions (@fig-study-area).

- **Romeo Malette Forest (RMF)** covers about 586,600 ha in the boreal forest of northeastern Ontario, near Timmins. Its low-relief terrain supports conifer and mixedwood stands dominated by black spruce, jack pine, trembling aspen and white birch. Stand structure is shaped by harvesting, wildfire, windthrow and insect outbreaks, so that stand edges are often sharp and reflect even-aged stands.

- **Ottawa Valley Forest (OVF)** covers about 806,200 ha in eastern Ontario, of which about 237,100 ha are managed Crown land, in the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence forest region. Its more rugged terrain supports a diverse mix of tolerant hardwoods, eastern hemlock, white and red pine, oak and intolerant hardwoods, managed under selection, shelterwood and clearcut systems. Changes between stands are often gradual and linked to species mixtures and partial harvesting.

Delineations were produced over each entire FMU. Their quality was assessed in four 50-ha validation areas per FMU (red dots in @fig-study-area), where drone LiDAR and field plots provided independent reference data (see [Data and Methods](data_and_method.qmd#performance-assessment)).

```{r}
#| label: fig-study-area
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Location of the Ottawa Valley Forest (A) and Romeo Malette Forest (B) forest management units in Ontario, with the four 50-ha validation areas of each unit (red dots)."
panel <- function(f, letter, buffer) {
  g <- filter(fmu, site == f)
  
  sat <- get_tiles(st_bbox(st_buffer(g, buffer)),
                   "Esri.WorldImagery", zoom = 11, crop = TRUE)
  
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster_rgb(data = sat*1.5) +
    geom_sf(data = g, color = "#FEFE62", fill = NA, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_sf(data = st_centroid(st_filter(dfa, g)), color = pal[["DFA"]],
            shape = 16, size = 2) +
    annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = letter, hjust = 1.6, vjust = 1.6,
             size = 8, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +    
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) + 
    annotation_scale(location = "br", width_hint = 0.28, style = "ticks",
                     tick_height = 1, line_width = 2, line_col = "white", 
                     text_col = "white", text_cex = 1, height = unit(0.15, "cm")) +
    theme_void()
}

A <- panel("OVF", "A", 13000)

B <- panel("RMF", "B", 5000)

global <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "grey88", color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = st_centroid(st_transform(fmu, 3979)), aes(color = site),
          shape = 16, size = 3.5) + 
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x = NA_real_, y = NA_real_, site = "DFA"),
             aes(x, y, color = site), shape = 16, size = 3.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_polygon(data = data.frame(x = NA_real_, y = NA_real_, k = "Forest management unit"),
                 aes(x, y, linetype = k), fill = NA, color = "#FEFE62", linewidth = 0.8,
                 inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(NULL, values = pal, labels = lab, limits = names(pal)) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(3979), default_crs = st_crs(4326), expand = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-170, -10, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(10, 80, 5)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text  = element_text(size = 5, color = "grey30"),
        panel.grid = element_line(linewidth = 0.2),
        legend.position     = "bottom",
        legend.direction    = "vertical",
        legend.justification = "center",
        legend.box          = "vertical",
        legend.box.just     = "left",
        legend.box.spacing  = unit(4, "pt"),
        legend.spacing.y    = unit(0, "pt"),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = alpha("white", 0.8), color = NA),
        legend.key        = element_blank(),
        legend.key.size   = unit(0.55, "cm"),
        legend.text       = element_text(size = 9),
        legend.margin     = margin(3, 5, 3, 3))

left <- global / plot_spacer() + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 0.5))
fig  <- (left | (A / B)) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.3))
fig
```

# **7** Acronyms {-#acronyms}

| Acronym | Meaning |
|---|---|
| EFI | Enhanced forest inventory: forest attributes predicted wall-to-wall from LiDAR |
| F1 | F1-score, a measure of agreement between stand boundaries and detected structural transitions |
| FMU | Forest management unit |
| FRI | Forest Resources Inventory (photo-interpreted stand polygons) |
| GRM | Generic Region Merging, the segmentation algorithm used to delineate stands |
| kNN | k-nearest neighbour imputation |
| OVF | Ottawa Valley Forest |
| PVE | Proportion of variance explained |
| QMDBH | Quadratic mean diameter at breast height |
| RMF | Romeo Malette Forest |
| S2 | Sentinel-2 satellite imagery |
| SMW | Split moving window analysis |
| SPL | Single-photon LiDAR (provincial airborne acquisition) |
| ULS | Uncrewed (drone) laser scanning |
| wSD | Area-weighted mean within-polygon standard deviation |
